newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. blocks WTO panel, urges EU rethink on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blocks WTO panel, urges EU rethink on Cuba.

text.p: The United States, arguing its national security interests were at stake, on Wednesday blocked a European Union request for a World Trade Organisation panel on the Helms-Burton law aimed at foreign investment in Cuba.

In a statement by its WTO ambassador Booth Gardner, Washington also appealed to Brussels to drop the case and join efforts to help bring about a switch to democracy on the communist-ruled Caribbean island.

But the EU signalled it would press ahead with its demand at the next meeting of the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) on November 20, saying the law aimed at using trade pressure to force other countries to line up behind U.S. foreign policy.

And reflecting the widespread condemnation around the world of the U.S. measures, WTO members from Asia and Latin America as well as non-EU Switzerland indicated backing for the complaint, declaring their concern at the law's "extra-territoriality."
Gardner told the DSB the Helms-Burton act, named after its authors in the U.S. Congress, was designed "to promote a swift transition to democracy in Cuba.

"Given the foreign policy and security concerns underpinning decades of U.S. relations with Cuba, and in the light of the common interests we share with our European friends in regard to Cuba, the United States is surprised and concerned to find our tactical and foreign policy differences over Cuba raised before a multilateral trade forum," the U.S. envoy declared.
Measures like the trade embargo imposed on Cuba over the past three decades had been expressly justified by Washington as pursuing "essential U.S. security interests," he said.

Arguing that the law in any case had minimal trade and investment effects on European interests, Gardner said the United States "would ask our European friends to think very carefully about whether to press their grievances over our Cuba policy towards this trade organisation."

The U.S. envoy spoke after the EU's acting head of mission to the WTO, Ian Wilkinson, said the law -- whose effect has been partially suspended by President Bill Clinton -- put up barriers to WTO accords on expanding trade and access to markets.
The 15-member EU, he said, objected "to the U.S. trying to force other countries to follow their own policy objectives through the threat and actual imposition of trade sanctions."

But in an apparent gesture of conciliation, there was no demand from Brussels for an extraordinary meeting of the DSB before the next scheduled meeting -- which comes well after the U.S. presidential elections on November 5.
Many of Clinton's Republican critics -- as well as some Democrats -- argue that Washington is allowing the WTO to bite into the U.S. sovereign right to set its own policies.

Under the procedures of the DSB, in whose creation the United States played a key role, a panel of three neutral experts will be automatically created at the next meeting of the body and will have six months to report its findings.

Although the U.S. has found almost no support, many trade diplomats and officials fear a ruling against Washington -- if confirmed by a later appeals board -- would boost U.S. opponents of the WTO and its system of global rule-making.

Voicing sympathy for the EU move on Wednesday were Washington's two partners in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) Mexico and Canada and Australia, India and Bolivia, speaking on behalf of most other Latin American states.
Cuba's ambassador Eumelio Caballero hailed the EU action as "praiseworthy", saying the Helms-Burton law violated "the rights of both my country and other member states of the WTO."
